node.label: Tony Judt
node.date_label: Past Imperfect (1992) · The Burden of Responsibility (1998) · Postwar (2005)
node.description: Historian of modern Europe whose Postwar joins Eastern and Western experiences through war’s consequences,political reconstruction and contested memory. In his interview with Donald Yerxa,Judt argues that selective forgetting enabled postwar national narratives and that European integration emerged through national interests. These are his interpretations,with differences across societies retained rather than a single story of inevitable liberal success.

incident_edges.relationship: Tony Judt: The Age of Extremes keeps the categories of the 1930s, gives Bolshevism “no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms”, devotes “just six pages” to “real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia and neglects nationalism (1995)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Judt (NYRB, 25 May 1995, read in full): the book's "defect, for there is really only one" is that "the categories right/left, fascist/Communist, progressive and reactionary seem to be very firmly set, and pretty much as they first presented themselves to Hobsbawm in the Thirties"; Bolshevism gets "no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms"; "“real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia merits just six pages"; the claim that Sovietisation followed American intervention "is simply wrong"; nationalism "is a rather neglected subject"; Hobsbawm "mostly avoids military or political narrative". Qualifications kept: Judt calls the book "a challenging, often brilliant, and always cool and intelligent account", praises its economic analysis and calls The Age of Capital "Hobsbawm’s single greatest work". The Age of Extremes itself is unread.

verification.note: Complete text and endnotes read for revision 1.147 (NYRB page; no pagination). A "Hobsbawm generation" of historians who began between about 1959 and 1975; Primitive Rebels "first appeared in 1959"; Labouring Men, Industry and Empire and Captain Swing "substantially recast the economic history of Britain and the story of the British labor movement"; the trilogy's scheme "eventually became the “conventional” interpretation"; The Age of Revolution 1962, The Age of Capital 1975 ("Hobsbawm’s single greatest work"), The Age of Empire twelve years later. Hobsbawm is "by training and inclination an economic historian, and an analytical one" who "mostly avoids military or political narrative"; "though unashamedly Eurocentric, Eric Hobsbawm has a unique range" (endnote 2 defends the European focus). The "one" defect: "the categories right/left, fascist/Communist, progressive and reactionary seem to be very firmly set, and pretty much as they first presented themselves to Hobsbawm in the Thirties"; Bolshevism gets "no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms"; "“real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia merits just six pages"; nationalism "is a rather neglected subject". Verdict: "a challenging, often brilliant, and always cool and intelligent account". The Age of Extremes itself is unread.
